text: Back in the Performance Tuning chapter, you learned the concepts: a clustered index defines a table's physical row order, a nonclustered index is a separate lookup structure with pointers. This lesson is the syntax companion to that idea — the actual CREATE INDEX statements behind it.

Create clustered index IX underscore LessonDemo underscore DemoID on dbo dot LessonDemo, DemoID. This physically sorts the table's rows by DemoID. Remember: a table can have only one clustered index, because the data can only be stored in one physical order at a time.

Create nonclustered index IX underscore LessonDemo underscore Label on dbo dot LessonDemo, Label. This builds a separate structure, sorted by Label, with pointers back to the actual rows. Unlike the clustered index, a table can have many nonclustered indexes.

Create nonclustered index on dbo dot LessonDemo, Label, include DemoID. Include adds DemoID to the index's leaf pages without making it part of the sort key. A query that filters on Label and only needs DemoID back can now be satisfied entirely from the index — this is called a covering index.
Only one clustered index is allowed per table — but any number of nonclustered indexes are fine, each one tuned for a different common lookup pattern your queries actually use.
